hero.name: Leela
hero.who: a 63-year-old retired school principal in Mysuru who thinks ageing is just bad luck

story.b: Leela retired two years ago as principal of a girls' high school in Mysuru. Since then she has slowed down. Her knees ache on the steps to her terrace garden. She misplaces her spectacles twice a day. She stopped going to the morning walking group at Kukkarahalli lake because she could not keep up. Whenever she mentions these things, friends say the same thing. It is just the age, what to do. Her mother had diabetes by sixty, so Leela assumes it is her fate too. Afternoons pass with TV serials, filter coffee and Mysore pak. When her grandson visits from Bengaluru and asks her to play badminton, she laughs and says those days are gone.

ask.q: Leela believes ageing is fate she can do nothing about. Which view would serve her better?
o: Some parts of ageing may be shaped by her daily habits, so trying is worth it
It is all in her genes, so any effort will change nothing
Try every new anti-ageing product she can find online
ask.why: Treating ageing as pure fate makes her stop trying, and online products promise far more than they can show. The book's view is that ageing may be a process we can influence. That gives her a reason to start with simple habits, guided by her doctor.

chapters.take: Ageing may be less fixed than you were told, so do not give up early.

story.b: At her routine check-up, Leela usually lists her complaints one by one. The knee. The sugar reading. The poor sleep. Each gets its own advice and its own tablet. This time she tries a different question. Is there anything she could do that might help many of these together? Her doctor smiles, as if she has waited years for a patient to ask. She talks about regular walking, simple strength exercises, more vegetables, steady sleep and fewer sweets. None of it is magic. But for the first time, Leela sees her body as one whole system, not a list of separate repairs. On the bus home, she quietly crosses out the word just in her head.

ask.q: Leela's friend Saroja says her knee pain is just age and nothing can be done. What should Leela suggest?
o: Agree, since aches at their age are simply natural
Order the knee supplement she saw advertised on TV
See a doctor and ask which habits could help her overall health
ask.why: Calling every problem just age stops people looking for help, and TV supplements skip proper advice. Asking a doctor about overall habits treats the body as one system, where a few steady changes may help several problems at once.

chapters.take: Ask what might help your whole body, not just one complaint.

story.b: In a magazine at the clinic, Leela reads about a theory that ageing may be partly a loss of information. The body's instructions mostly stay intact, the article says, but the system that reads them gets messier over time. Leela, a teacher for thirty-five years, thinks of an old attendance register. Every name is still there, but after years of handling, the marks get smudged and hard to read. It is only a theory, still being studied, she reminds herself. But it makes her curious about what might smudge the pages faster. She looks at her own days. Six hours of sitting with serials. Sweets with every coffee. She writes one habit down: sitting too long.

ask.q: Leela reads that ageing may be the body slowly losing its instructions. What is a sensible way to use this idea?
o: Treat it as proven fact and buy tests that claim to measure it
Use it as a nudge to look at which daily habits might wear her down
Dismiss it completely, since she is not a scientist
ask.why: The idea is a theory still being studied, so treating it as proven and paying for costly tests goes too far. Dismissing it wastes a useful nudge. Using it to look honestly at her habits, like hours of sitting, is a sensible, low-risk step.

chapters.take: Treat new theories as nudges to check your habits, not as proven facts.

story.h: Stairs, the lake and a bag
story.b: Leela starts adding small challenges to her day. She climbs the stairs to her terrace garden twice each morning instead of once. She rejoins the walking group at Kukkarahalli lake, walking briskly for the first round and slowly for the second. She carries her own vegetable bag back from Devaraja market. Her doctor showed her two simple knee exercises, and she does them while the coffee decoction drips. At first her legs feel heavy and she is tired by evening, but it is a good tiredness. One day her knee aches more than usual, so she rests and mentions it at her next visit. Slowly, the stairs begin to feel shorter.

ask.q: Leela feels mild tiredness after her new walks and stairs. What should she do?
o: Stop completely, since any strain at her age must be harmful
Double the effort at once to speed up the benefits
Keep the mild challenge, build up slowly, and see her doctor if pain appears
ask.why: Mild, steady challenge like brisk walks and stairs is the kind of helpful stress the book describes. Stopping at the first tiredness loses that, and doubling at once risks injury. Building slowly, and asking her doctor about real pain, keeps it safe.

chapters.take: A little healthy challenge, built up slowly, may help the body repair.

story.b: Leela notices she eats almost all day. Biscuits with coffee at eleven, bajji at four, Mysore pak after dinner. She has read that eating less often, with more plants, may help the body. But she takes tablets for blood pressure, and her sugar is borderline, so she does not try anything on her own. She takes her idea to her doctor. Together they make a careful plan. Regular meals stay. The eleven o'clock biscuits and the four o'clock bajji go. Her plate gets more greens, ragi, dal and vegetables, and the Mysore pak becomes a Sunday treat. After a few weeks, Leela feels lighter, and her afternoons are less sleepy.

ask.q: Leela takes BP tablets and wants to start skipping meals. What should she do?
o: Start skipping lunch every day, since less food must always be better
Check with her doctor first, then make careful changes like cutting snacks
Stop her BP tablets for a while to let her body reset
ask.why: Skipping meals while on medicines can be risky, and stopping BP tablets on her own could be dangerous. Less food is not always better. Her doctor knows her health and can help her choose safe changes, like fewer snacks and more plants.

chapters.take: Eat less often and more plants, but only with your doctor's advice.

story.b: A message spreads through Leela's retired teachers' WhatsApp group. It praises a new supplement that claims to reverse ageing, at three thousand rupees a month. Her friend Saroja has already ordered two boxes. Leela feels the pull. Who would not want to feel younger? Then she remembers what she has read. Much of this research is early, often done in animals, and scientists still argue about it. At her next check-up, she shows the message to her doctor. The doctor explains that the evidence in people is not settled, and that some supplements can interact with her BP tablets. Leela decides to spend the money on good walking shoes and more fruit instead.

ask.q: A friend forwards a supplement that claims to reverse ageing. What should Leela do?
o: Ask her doctor about it before taking anything at all
Order it, since it is everywhere online and must work
Buy it for her friends too, so they all age slower together
ask.why: Much of the excitement comes from early research, often in animals, and supplements can interact with her tablets. Being popular online does not make something safe or effective. Her doctor can weigh it against her health before she spends money or swallows anything.

chapters.take: Exciting science is still unfolding. Ask your doctor before you buy into it.

story.b: By the Dasara holidays, Leela's days look different. She walks at the lake four mornings a week with her old group, who tease her for walking faster than them. She takes the stairs without thinking. Her plate has more greens, the afternoon snacks are gone, and Mysore pak waits for Sunday. Her doctor is pleased with her last check-up and has asked her to keep going. When her grandson visits, he hands her a badminton racket as a joke. Leela takes it. They play for fifteen minutes on the colony road, and she laughs at her own misses. She still forgets her spectacles. But when someone says it is just the age, she smiles.

chapters.take: Small daily habits, guided by your doctor, are a real way to age well.
